description: react-component-development is targeted against three route components that each hand-roll their own loading and error branches in three different shapes — PostListPage.tsx inline, PostEditorPage.tsx by early return, RootRedirect.tsx by early return that renders nothing at all while pending — with code-maintainability (a general-quality read of the same repetition) and react-component-styling (a misroute, since nothing about the repetition is CSS) sitting in the peer set as competing, plausible-looking picks, which is what makes the discovery factor a real question rather than a formality. The outcome factors check that the repeated concern lands in one new module both PostListPage.tsx and PostEditorPage.tsx import, and that the extraction still lets each screen say its own thing rather than flattening both onto one hardcoded message. Neither factor asserts role="alert" or any other semantic or keyboard detail: react-component-development's own SKILL.md defers semantics and keyboard behaviour to a high-fidelity UI design capability, and none is in this scenario's peer set, so asserting one would measure accessibility instinct with nothing to attribute the result to.

task.prompt: Right now every screen in the console handles "still loading" and "that didn't work" in its own way — the post list prints one sentence, the editor replaces the whole screen with a different one, and opening the app shows nothing at all for a moment. None of them quite matches the others. We're adding a couple more screens soon and I'd rather each one didn't invent its own version of this all over again.

factors.description: The ask names neither react-component-development nor the mechanism a fix would use, only three screens that each handle "still loading" and "that didn't work" differently — an agent that reaches for react-component-development here is finding it from the problem, with code-maintainability (a general-quality read of the same repetition) and react-component-styling (a misroute, since nothing about the repetition is CSS) sitting right there as competing, plausible-looking picks.

Reads PostListPage.tsx and PostEditorPage.tsx from the reconstructed workspace, resolves each file's relative imports, and takes the SET of resolved modules imported by both that are also files this probe's own diff added. Requires that set, taken together rather than any one file alone, to be actually about loading and error: a loading-ish token (pending/loading/waiting/busy/fetching/spinner/skeleton) and a failure-ish token (isError/hasError/failure/problem/retry/alert/a rendered role="alert", among others — never a bare "error", which almost any module contains unrelated to this concern) found somewhere across the set. Two focused components — a Spinner and a separate ErrorBanner, each newly added and shared — satisfy this exactly as well as one combined component does. A module that is nothing but a bare re-export is read as the file it names instead, one hop; a module this cannot fully resolve counts in its favour rather than against it, and a module that merely references both concerns without truly consolidating them can pass on lexical presence alone — both deliberate: a false negative here rejects a probe that extracted correctly, landing specifically on the skill-present arm, the worse of this instrument's two possible errors; a false positive costs one over-generous verdict, symmetric across both conditions. A shared .module.css never counts, since a stylesheet says nothing about the repeated BEHAVIOUR this scenario is about. Two screens that each grew their own helper, introduced no new file, or share a module unrelated to loading and error all still fail it. A route file missing from the workspace is a judgment this script cannot make, so it exits non-zero rather than reporting false.

The paired "must not disappear" factor. react-component-development's own component-states.md has the shared surface take its content from the caller so features "keep their distinct control without forking the surface"; an extraction that renders one hardcoded message on both screens has moved the duplication rather than removed it. The script finds the same shared, newly-added module SET the factor above detects, reads each screen's own usage of every module in it, and reports false when the two screens' combined usage is identical once each screen's own pre-existing query-variable name is normalized away — including when there is no such module set to parameterize at all. It is deliberately not independent of the factor above, judging the quality of the extraction that factor detects, so a run that changed nothing also passes it — the same reason keeps-the-detail-cache-write and keeps-the-animation-for-everyone-else are declared as pairs for their own scenarios. It inherits that factor's own permissive bias: a module accepted on lexical presence alone, without truly consolidating the concern, is still compared for usage the same as any other.
